speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) has carefully studied the issue, including the arrangements in other countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The calls for portability of IPs stem mainly from three groups of policyholders: those who are unhappy with changes in the terms of their policy coverage imposed by their insurer; those who faced difficulties in making claims; and those who find it difficult to afford their IP premiums as they become older.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Hence, they want to switch to another plan offered by another insurer but realised that they have to undergo another round of underwriting and may not be able to preserve the coverage they already have or they have to pay more premiums.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The conclusion is that IP portability – allowing all IP policyholders to switch insurers freely – will enhance competition and improve bargaining power of IP policyholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: IP portability is generally uncommon across the world, as it is usual practice for insurers to underwrite new policies in order to price the risks of accepting more policyholders with pre-existing conditions into their risk pool.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Underwriting can result in the insurer imposing additional conditions on the policyholder’s coverage, such as a waiting period during which no claims will be paid or exclusions to the coverage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Policyholders may also have to pay higher premiums in view of the higher risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For countries that ensure full portability where policyholders can switch insurers without underwriting, it is usually a feature limited to their mandatory, national health insurance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, in the case of the Netherlands or Switzerland, universal coverage is mandated but administered by private insurers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These private insurers are, therefore, required to accept any applicant, regardless of whether they are switching from another insurer or are uninsured previously.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This gives the impression that the commercial insurance is portable, but actually it is not, as only the basic coverage under the universal, national health insurance scheme is fully portable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These countries do have supplemental, private insurance, which involves underwriting and is not portable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As our national health insurance scheme, MediShield Life covers all residents, regardless of age, health status, personal insurance or employer coverage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This ensures that all residents enjoy a basic level of protection against large hospital bills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will continue to ensure that MediShield Life stays relevant and affordable to Singaporeans as our national health insurance scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Australia and Ireland are two notable examples that have implemented full portability for non-national, supplemental private health insurance plans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: But they did so for different reasons than one may think.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In Australia, private hospital care accounts for close to half of admissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: So, good uptake of private health insurance, including through features like full portability, is integral to support access.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As for Ireland, private insurance was initially introduced for a population segment who was not eligible to receive free treatment under their public healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Private insurance with full portability was established to ensure that the segment previously mentioned had protection against large bills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This feature continued to be retained even as policy reforms later extended universal access to public hospital care to this group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In all instances where full portability between private insurers is ensured, whether in the Netherlands, Switzerland, Australia or Ireland, additional compensation mechanisms need to be established.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In other words, for insurance company A to take over from insurance company B, a policyholder with a pre-existing condition and of higher risk, A will receive compensation from B.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To facilitate this compensation system, countries set up a risk equalisation fund, usually funded with public monies and insurer contributions and where a neutral body facilitates transfer payments between insurers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Insurers with a lower-than-average risk profile provide net funding into the fund while insurers with a higher-than-average risk profile receive net funding from the fund.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Significant additional national resources will need to be set up and to administer the fund.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: If we do this, it will be a whole new department.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Most of all, it is not an international best practice for supplementary and commercial personal health insurance to be fully portable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Fundamentally, for the group of IP policyholders with pre-existing conditions, the issue may not be a lack of competition among insurers, but that insurers are not actively competing for this group of customers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: It is because their probability of claims is higher, which means that insurers may have to pay out to them more than what they collect in premiums.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The best way to provide assurance to everyone is to keep healthcare costs manageable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Health)
text: At the national level, MOH will continue to look at measures to manage healthcare costs and ensure that all Singaporeans have access to good and affordable basic healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If I may just have some preamble to frame some of the issues my residents in Clementi face, followed by supplementary questions, and I beg Speaker's indulgence.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, I have residents who ask if the insurers have moved the goalposts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, the doctor now must be on a panel, but the criteria are not always clear.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, the insurer has changed the access to policy benefits or how the coverage is administered.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Minister of State, notwithstanding the difficulties with portable IP insurers, does the Minister of State agree that these challenges faced by middle-aged Singaporeans, existing policyholders, are real in their lived experience?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And will MOH, therefore, keep a close watch on the insurers, their profit margins and how they approach these policyholders?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Lastly, if I may quote Minister Ong Ye Kung who, on 27 April 2024, was reported in The Straits Times online as saying, he "really hope the insurance industry takes a hard look at the fundamental design of their policies, their riders, how to make it sustainable for the long term".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Does the Minister of State agree that there are policyholders who did not ask to be sold products which were unsustainable, and if it can be proven that some insurers sold products knowing the products would be unsustainable someday, does that change the weight of thinking and support towards these policyholders more?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They cannot compete for the market to the point that they then are unable to sustain the product, which is what is happening now.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: To the Member's question as to whether we can scrutinise this, we are indeed scrutinising it quite intently and this is because we are seeing some of these challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Member also raised the issue of moving of the goalposts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I will make a few points in this respect.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is what are the terms in the contract that parties had agreed upon.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And the response and the motivation by the insurance company is then to actually create these products to cater to all these expectations of the customers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But the third point, the more important point, is really this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We need to understand that at the national level, this will all cost and contribute to higher costs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: That is the key thing that we need to look at because the change in terms is really a sign of this happening.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Insurers need to take a step back and renew their fundamental designs of their schemes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It cannot be about enhancing the payouts to get the market share and when the sums do not work out, then they adjust the terms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, that is the point that the Minister for Health was trying to address and that is indeed why we are calling for a fundamental redesign of the system.
